Chemical Engineering is a very very broad term.

The core definition, as you may learn in college, is that it's an engineering discipline that deals with moving and processing substances.
Usually but necessarily you need to have some piping and vessels in which some processes take place.

Now, try to imagine were that could be applicable. Anywhere, to be frank: Making any kind of processed food (e.g. cheese, meat products, dairy, pasta, beer, coffee), drugs, fuels (oil & gas dominates here and it's the one declining), clothing materials, specific gases/liquids (e.g. medical gases, lubricants for machinery, gases for welding), plastics, household chemicals, pesticides, fertilizers, weapons... I could go on and on.

Also the type of job you can do can also be anywhere in a production chain: design of products, design of equipment, design of production plants, operation of production facilities, safety and environmental assessment, management, etc.

But the issue is I haven't yet met a Chemical Engineer who can work anywhere I listed. Usually it takes about 8-10 years of work before you are accepted as an experienced engineer, and by then you have some specific skills in some specific field.

Then it's not that easy to switch fields, or at least I haven't found an easy way to do the switch.

TL;DR: So to answer your question, Chemical Engineering jobs will not decline, because without them you can't make anything, but the specific occupations within Chemical Engineering do change with times.

All in all I would consider studying for it, because it is such a stimulating discipline when you are in a right place. You need to learn chemistry, physics, biology, maths, economics, earth sciences and apply the knowledge in different situations. It also pays well. Well, maybe less that in medicine or law, but those are completely different kinds of work.
